Basically, they were reminding everyone of the various rules around the office. Like not loitering during office hours, sticking to our lunch schedules, the correct dress code, wearing of IDs at all times etc. In my 6 month stay here our HR hasn't issued me an office ID card. Despite their large number of employees (they have an entire floor to themselves unlike multiple departments in one floor), they are slow. They took about 5 months to process my payroll alone, so the delay in ID cards are not a surprise to us. Everyone without an office ID just started using government issued IDs to be able to enter our building but this morning, security started telling everyone that starting next week anyone without an ID will have their names be noted and be reported to HR. I promptly called HR when I got to my desk to ask for a status for my (and my other colleagues) ID. They told me that they can't print our IDs yet because the team in charge is swarmed with other "projects" and suggested that we can print our own IDs, and gave us the template. My colleagues and I disagreed with this. We argued that we don't want to make up for the short comings of HR, by shelling out money from our own pockets to print our IDs, and that it should have been provided to us in the first place. We plan on just keep using whatever IDs we have right now be damned whatever happens next week. So, AITA for disagreeing with our HR?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's right or wrong for me to disagree with HR in this situation. Let me start by understanding the scenario. I'm a 7-month newly hired employee at a big corporation. Last night, HR sent out a five-page memo titled "Office Discipline." They reminded everyone about various office rules, like not loitering during office hours, sticking to lunch schedules, dress code, and wearing IDs at all times. Now, in my 6 months here, HR hasn't issued me an office ID card. The company is big, with an entire floor for HR, unlike other departments that share floors. Despite their size, they're slow. It took them about 5 months to process my payroll, so the delay in ID cards isn't a surprise. Everyone without an office ID started using government-issued IDs to enter the building. But this morning, security announced that starting next week, anyone without an ID will have their names noted and reported to HR. I called HR when I got to my desk to ask about the status of my ID and my colleagues'. They said they can't print our IDs yet because the team in charge is swamped with other "projects" and suggested we print our own IDs using a template they provided. My colleagues and I disagreed. We argued that we shouldn't have to make up for HR's shortcomings by spending our own money to print IDs, especially since it should have been provided in the first place. We decided to keep using whatever IDs we have right now, regardless of what happens next week. So, the question is: Is it right or wrong for me to disagree with HR in this situation? First, I need to consider the company's policies. The memo clearly states that IDs must be worn at all times. HR is responsible for issuing these IDs. However, they've been slow and have not provided them despite the policy. HR suggested that employees print their own IDs, which seems like a workaround for their inefficiency. My colleagues and I feel that this is unfair because we shouldn't have to cover the costs or take the time to print IDs ourselves. On one hand, following company policies is important. Security is enforcing the ID rule, and without an official ID, we might face consequences. On the other hand, HR's failure to provide IDs in a timely manner is a systemic issue. I think it's reasonable to push back against HR's suggestion because it's essentially shifting their responsibility onto employees. It's not fair for employees to bear the burden of HR's inefficiency. However, we also need to comply with the security policy to avoid any negative repercussions. Maybe a better approach would be to escalate the issue. Instead of just disagreeing, we could request a meeting with HR to discuss the delays and the burden it's causing. We could also ask for a timeline for when the IDs will be ready. In the meantime, using government-issued IDs might be a temporary solution, but it's important to communicate our concerns clearly. Disagreeing with HR is justified in this case because they're not fulfilling their responsibilities, but we should do so respectfully and seek a resolution rather than just refusing to comply without any further action. So, considering all this, I think it's right to disagree with HR because they're not meeting their obligations, but it's also important to find a constructive way to address the issue rather than just refusing to comply without trying to resolve it.
